blocks.x: Okay, let me see. Let me ask you your name first so we'll know for sure.
Well, the whole name or just part of it?
Well, just the name that you use in the music. Okay, Don Albert. And what is your right name, your full name?
Don Albert Dominique.

Oh, I see. It was originally Albert Dominique, I think you called it. That is correct. Yeah, okay. You can just lean back and relax. Yeah. I think it's going okay. And we're at 910 Royal Street. This is my apartment. And I forgot to get the date down. What's the date?
Today is the 30th of December.
Almost.
Almost Happy New Year.
Almost Happy New Year. Alright.

Well, let's see. We're going to talk about a whole lot of different things, like I'd gotten a letter from Laurie Wright, and he wanted a little more information on Lewis Armstrong. Where did you first hear Louis Armstrong?

Well, as far back as I can remember, when I was a little kid, when this particular group of boys would parade on the streets, I'd break my neck to go over there and listen to them. And sometimes they came right down to San Antonio Street, which was about, well, in between the two blocks that I lived. I lived on Robinson and the parade would come down San Antonio Street. I don't know, I don't know, they had a hymn there. How did that happen? What were they doing? Well, just parading, I imagine. I can't recall exactly what it was for, but as far as I can recall, it was just a parade. As this city of New Orleans is known for the parades and also for the advertising bands that used to ride around on the wagons.

And was that for a school or something? How did that happen? Yes, it was for Jones. Oh, for Jones. That's right. A wave song. A wave song. I see. Well, now, did you get to know him down here? Did you meet him later?
No, I met a lawyer in later years after I had gotten my band and we met, and through other musicians I met there. We became real, real close friends.
And another thing he asked me about it was this Wabash Blues was supposed to be out by Troy Floyd, I guess.

Now, that's a little controversial there. Yeah. As far as I know, Troy did not make this Wabash Blues, but I have a copy of it at my home in San Antonio. I can't recall who the musicians on there just by playing it, but it seems to me that I can remember that I was part of that Wabash Blues, I'm not for sure, and also Charlie Dixon. When we recorded all these numbers, even with Hattie Brothers and the whole group, I think we recorded about three or four days. And the same musicians that were on these recordings are the ones that were on this Wabash, this particular label, Wabash Blues, but I just can't, I'm going to have to play it over again and see if I can't listen to it a little more closely.
Well, tell me a little bit more about Troy Floyd's band. I don't know too much about it, it's what you've told me.

Well, the history of Troy Floyd's band goes way back to the days of Alfonso Trent, who was a band that was organized with Texas musicians and Arkansas, because Trent originally was from a little town of Fort Smith, Arkansas. His estate was still there, I visited the estate just a couple of three years ago. And Trent was playing at the Adolphus Hotel, incidentally the first name of a band to be put into one of these big establishments. So Troy had his band organized with mostly Texas men. And the great trumpet player that was in his band, Ben O'Kennedy, quit Troy's band in Galveston. And I got worried about him leaving the band through Chester Clark, who was the trumpet player with Trent, wonderful trumpet player, tremendous. He said, you should wire Troy Floyd because he'll need a man in that seat and he'll fit it. I had my little three piece band and they joined another couple of musicians in Dallas. So I decided just to take a chance because my goal was set to become a great musician. And I tried and he asked me to wait for him that he would interview me when he got to Dallas. So I told the boys in the band that I thought I was going to quit them and I received them that they got back to New Orleans or do whatever they wanted to do. I could try to get them a job in another band if they wanted to stay around Texas. So they decided it would be better for them to come back to New Orleans. So Troy didn't listen to me play. He just put me in the automobiles and went out to East Texas to Eastland. And that was the first time that he heard me just tune my horn. He said, man, what a beautiful sound. How did I do it? And I said, well, I'm not. And incidentally, I was only 17 years old. So I got the job from just him and him. He blew my horn. And he was a man. He became the first chair man, also the feature man, because out of 10 musicians, I don't think there was about three or four of us that could be considered readers.
Well, how did he play then? Did he use many head arrangements? Would he just be faking all the time or what? I don't know.

A lot of head arrangements and the piano player was a good reading musician, not a hell of a piano player, but a good reading musician. Then he had, well, Ben O'Kennedy, who was the trumpet player, was a seasoned musician. He was great. And I imagined through him and the piano player and the drummer who could read and Charlie Dixon, who could read. And Troy was a good reader. Troy could read, but he wasn't much of a player, but a good reader. And that way they got together and they rehearsed the numbers and I guess just naturally they knew what they were doing.

In listening to their recordings, you know, of the Shadowland and Dreamland blues, I had to hear things, it sounds like they're doing a lot of playing by ear. They are. On those particular recordings.

There weren't any written arrangements as far as that's concerned, unless it was what we call stock arrangements. And everybody didn't read? No. In fact when they were playing, when we had to play the big shows with Troy S. Ben, I had to use the piano part, the violin part, the trumpet part, and the clarinet part. And Pete jumped from one to the other to fit in to make the music right for the performance we were playing for. Could you transpose it? Sure, I can transpose it aside. I can transpose it from a violin part, from a clarinet part, or from a piano part. Also from an alto part.
You learn something new every day.

You see, I studied the music, which was something in my favor. As I always said, the background of the family is very musical. My grandmother and grandfather were singers. Had a knot that played the piano. One uncle that played the violin. One played the cornet. Two of them because Natty is still living. And he doesn't play anymore. He still has his horn. But even on, we can go back and just name just schools or something that wasn't in the family that were musically inclined. And I hope that that's where I got mine from. Because I find this, that my son and my daughter doesn't even know the music. Had never been interested in it.
What about Natty? Did you know Natty Dominique when he was down here?

Oh, sure. Uncle Natty and I were, he was one of my favorite uncles. He was the younger one. Uncle Natty. And Uncle Natty went to war. And he was a mutilary in the war. And I remember the first time he came back. And he came to the estate up there on Grey Court Street. He didn't stay too long. And he left in Chicago. And I visited him quite a number of times. After I got my band. And I'd go and play up in the eastern part of the states. And Uncle Natty would be one of the first ones that I would go to see him. Samuel and Bonnie. Bonnie left a couple of years before I did in this Bonnie Biggore. Well, I'd visit Bonnie in New York or wherever I was. Right across him.
Did you, in playing, back in the chorus band, in playing stock arrangements and everything, did they change them around much? Not very much. You wouldn't put your own?
Only introductions, choruses, and the quarters, and back to the chorus and out.

Mm-hmm. I see. So some of the guys would be faking, but the others would read their parts. That's right. And not, you didn't try to make it anything special, just like it was written. I see. What happened to Charlie Dixon?

Charlie Dixon passed about three or five years ago. He died in San Antonio, Texas. He was a wonderful musician and a great fellow. In fact, Charlie Dixon was more of a father to the band. Everybody looked up at Charlie Dixon as an advisor. And he was exceptionally crazy about me. He used to call me Big Jim. Why, I don't know, but that's what he, Monarchy, laid on me.
I wondered about that band. A whole lot of things, you know. He seemed to have a quite unusual style. I never heard anybody else play trombone quite like Charlie Dixon.

Well, Charlie Dixon wasn't on the trombone play. His main instrument was the tuba. And that got along on the trombone. And both of them, he'd get a tremendous tone. Willie Long also was a fairly good reader. And so was Benny. Benny wasn't a real fast reader, but they were what we call spellers. And you get together with these guys that can read little and you knowing how it should go when you play it for them and they'd get it on you. Well, it wouldn't take long to run these arrangements down and get them. Well, then they had pretty good ears. Good ears. For instance, this fellow, Scott Bagby. Scott Bagby played a tremendous piano. Up until today, I don't believe Scott Bagby would know one note from the other. But he would put a sheet of music in front of him and it's remarkable. When the notes went up, he went up. When he came down, he finally was getting the perfect harmony. He still lived in his way up in the seventies. He's a very active man. He plays church music now. Where does he live? He lives in San Antonio.
Well, do you know where he got his style? I was especially curious because of what Gunther Schiller had to say in his book.

I think, I'm not passing any criticism. I think there's a little misinformation there. Scott Bagby is just one of these natural musicians. And his playing was just a gift to him. And after he played the clarinet and he got into Troy's band, and by doubling their playing was just one of their first-minded families. But for their first- bamboo traveling and he decided well he's going to do something else so he quits and you have to replace him.
Yeah there were a lot of changes in that band you told him at once I mean.

Men would come and go. No not too many in that band. My band had a lot of changes but not Troy's band. They only changed, well after yes after I left he started to change a lot of musicians to try to keep the remnants going. But when I was there it was almost a family affair because we all worked together with each other. And Scott Bagley was the only one that I could remember that dropped out and got a replacement with Herschel Evans. Because Fred Murphy didn't want to leave Dallas, Texas I tried to get Fred to join the band. Fred he didn't want to, he played a few days with us until we could get a replacement.
Did he play alcohol or tennis? Alton.
Alton. Alton the soprano.
Well anyway, what was Scott Bagley's nickname? Funny. Funny huh?
F-U-N-N-Y, because he was a funny man. What did he do? Just comical and funny. Little bit of fella, little small guy. Did some funny things.
Do you remember any of them that would come back to your memory now or not?
Sure. Like who?
Just anything that he did that would be funny. Oh you mean Scott?

Yeah. No, he was a fella that couldn't take kiddin' so much and I was a young boy and we'd do little funny tricks on him and he would get mad and he'd blow his stack and he'd be alright after. But that was the nickname, Funnies.
Well what about Herschel Evans then? Was he a good reader when he came?

No, Herschel couldn't read music. How I met Herschel Evans, I was getting ready to leave here and they used to have the Dixie Series and there was a band that Herschel came here with, with a team from Wichita Falls that year. The name of this band was the TNT band and Jimmy Westbrook was the drummer, he's a left-handed drummer. He's now living in Los Angeles and Herschel was playing alto and playing a date up at the old Pelican ball and I met Herschel then and we all left on the same train. I was going to Dallas then with my three piece band and they asked me to blow my horn for them because they liked the tone that I had got out the horn so we became real close friends. When we got to Dallas we split up and went different ways and after I joined Troy's band, that's when we were playing in Wichita Falls and I happened to see Herschel coming down the street and that's the time that we needed the man in the band and Fred was playing that day with us in Wichita Falls. So I asked Herschel, I said, man what are you doing here? He says, I'm on a circus. I said, circus? What are you playing? He said, well I'm playing tennis. I said, can you read yet? He said, no I haven't learned yet. He said, but I can play, he said, like all the numbers that Prince and McCormick Hawkins were playing Stampede and the numbers that Henderson had. He said, I'll play it just like him. I said, I'm going to sit you down in the chair and I'll call the numbers tonight. I'm going to call everything I know you can play. You'll have to let on the children how to read. And sure enough he went ahead and blowed the roof off and got the job and we became real close friends and I'd help him. He had a knack of playing the piano and I had a good idea of one finger. So I taught him his notes and showed him how to read and became a fairly good reader.
Did he play much clarinet?

No, he couldn't. He couldn't play clarinet. But he'd blow on it. What kind of circus bands did they have then? Regular traveling bands like Ole Miss, I can't recall the name of them, out of Georgia and Alabama. Stock shows that traveled around playing for the singers, blues singers. During the olden days that was the way they earned their living, going around on these circus fields.
What about the battles of music that you had with the Troy Floyd?

That used to be a gate attraction. Never was a winner, never was a loser. I remember we played one with George Lee, who was from Kansas City. George had a tremendous band. And George was a great singer, George E. Lee. That's Julia Lee's brother. Well, we packed the place, two bands, and we walked off as winners, I guess. Then later on, years of my band, I had a lot of battle of bands. Because that was one way of enticing the public in.
I know you tell me about meeting many different people. What about Walter Page?

Now, which one? You have more than one Walter Page. I'm talking about the bass player. Oh, the bass player. That was the original Blue Devils. And he had Orrin, Kid Lips Page, that was in the same band. And also Count Basin.
Did you ever meet up with them?
Met those in Dallas.
And did you have battles with them?
Yes, we had battles with them, and also jammed together after hours. Orrin Lips Page was one of the really great trumpet players, too. I think he died a few years ago in England.
Yes, he's dead now. That's right. Were these, you'd say Troy Floyd's band was a happy band, or they were all happy together?

Right, right. The name of the band was Troy Floyd and his orchestra of gold. Everybody had gold instruments. And I never, I should have kept this, but I don't know why I didn't. C.G. Kahn made me a present of the first long trumpet that was made. And they carried my name on the little pamphlets in my picture, showing that I blew nothing but C.G. Kahn instruments. I never did keep this. I should have. Do you still play Kahn? No, I'm not playing a Selma. But I have nothing against C.G. Kahn. I think it's a tremendous instrument.
Say you were going to meet up with them back at the Battle of New. Say you were going to meet up with somebody, would you rehearse before you met?
No, you just go play your regular O-T music. Just like you play everyone. It was just a gimmick to bring the people in.

Did Troy Floyd's band rehearse much? Quite a bit. Quite a bit of rehearsals. Every day or a week? Two or three times a week. And what kind of leader was Floyd? Was he a good salesman? What about being on the stand?

Well, the fella's dead man. You know, you don't talk about a dead man. All in all, Troy was, to me, was a nice fella. Had some bad faults that a band leader shouldn't have had. What I imagined in those days, what he did was just normal reaction to a man that became partly famous. We had our differences.
Did they have brass bands over there like they do here?

No brass bands at all. It was amazing to me when I would try to figure out why. And I never could. And the first time that I ever heard a brass band after I left New Orleans was here. It was many years later up in the little town of Columbia, South Carolina. It wasn't like the bands down here, but it still was a marching band. And they were marching behind one of these prophets, Daddy Grace. And I ran about five blocks to get to hear a marching band.
Were they reading straight or did they play by ear or not?
No, I'm asking these guys who found a good musician because they had seen it though. There were some guys out of college or out of schools around there and they had to be good musicians.
I never have heard any brass bands that sounded like New Orleans brass bands anywhere except on records. They have some over in England.

Well the only time you would hear anything that would resemble a New Orleans band, which was very, very rare and scarce, if a bunch of the New Orleans musicians got together, say for instance in Chicago or somewhere in the area where they were congregated and organized some of it. Otherwise you never would find it like here.
And who were some of the great Southwestern bands?

Well now there were quite a number of those bands and I just can't recall all of them. The two to the name were the outstanding ones, Troy and Trent. Of course in Galveston, Texas you had a band named Lazy Daddy's Band. Then you had the Royal Garden Band that left from Texas and went to California, which was another tremendous pioneer band. And Eddie Hewitt's daddy would come through there. He was a piano player. But there weren't too many big bands. Most of them concentrated on three, four and five piece combos.
What was the Royal Garden Band?
The Royal Garden was about seven or eight pieces.
Who had it?
Edgar Perry, a piano player. A tremendous piano player, Edgar Perry.
I never heard of him.

Well, the history behind him is kind of vague. I don't know of too many people that can recall Edgar Perry. Some of them in San Antonio do recall him and they remember him playing and leaving. The musicians that would know him would be like A.J. Johnson and he's past.
So there's just a band that disappeared from the scene. That's right. Maybe you could find something in California or something.

Possibly so, more than likely in Texas if you could ever find someone that knew Eddie Perry. Did Troy Floyd have a theme? Yes, Troy's theme was, oh, let's go a little further. You have to come in. I'm afraid. I'm afraid someday you'll leave. I'm afraid someday I'll breathe. I'm afraid. It was a beautiful song. And Troy would do a spiel on it. He would talk it. Like what's this guy does is talking on his numbers. He'd sing and then he'd talk it a lot. One of the old, old timers. One of the white... I don't know.
There'd been several. Ted Lewis. There you go. You hit it right on the head. He was like, do that kind of thing?
Yeah, like Ted Lewis.
So he was a showman and a salesman type of guy? He tried to be. Yeah.
But he was more of a gaminer, I'll put it that way.
Well, he must have known the right people if he found jobs by him.
Oh, yes. He could get the jobs.
Back to New Orleans in the early days, what did George Moret sound like?

George Moret was a rough, well, I'll explain it in musical terms, a rough trumpet player. Very good musician. Old man George Moret lived about three or four blocks from my house in the family. Real close friends through my grandfather and my father. And George could read music and actually he came from the old school or the old professors too. But he was loud and rough, if I can recall real well. Because when I went to, when George would take me on the jobs with him, I was only in the area of a lot of ten, twelve years old.
Do you remember him as playing any jazz or remember him as a brass band? Well, yes.
Mostly like they played in Manu Perez and guys like that played practically the same type of trumpet.
Do you remember who was in George Moret's bands?
No, I can't recall anybody there. Unless someone would refresh my memory of it, then I could remember.
Well, as a kid, could you get out late at night or anything?
Well, my daddy would let me go with all the musicians and they would take me home.

Well, you were playing professional jobs quite young is what I'm getting to. About fourteen years old. And so you wouldn't get arrested then? Oh, no. No laws against working with the kid? No, no laws against working with the kid.
Not here in Louisiana.
Your father then must have known the people you went out with. Oh, yes, you know.
So did my mother. And sometimes she came over and waited for me to take me home. For instance, when the boat docked over on this side of the lake where she or my daddy would be waiting for me.
What time would the boat get back?

Those hours were very vague in my mind. If I can remember well, they'd leave early in the morning. They would get over to Mandeville or Covington and they would spend three or four hours over there. The people would get off the boat and go around town and then picnics underneath the trees. Then they would leave and it seems as though the boat would get back here between six and seven o'clock just about dusk.
So you didn't have to worry about the nine o'clock bell?
No, not that time.
Was there really a nine o'clock bell?
Yes, it was. When I was courting my wife, I was ready to get engaged to my wife and at nine o'clock, if I wasn't home, my daddy was on the corner blowing that whistle for me to get home.

So you had a fairly good age even then. That's right. When you went over across the lake into Susquehanna, I think you wrote to Ropeman you went to Mandeville, and then Buddy had a place. In Covington.

To Covington. Right. In Covington. Buddy had an old shack way back in the woods. What would you all talk about? Well, just everything in general. We'd be cooking on his stove and I would share some of his vittles with him, talk about music and at regular procedure, how I'm doing and how you're doing and so forth and so on.
But would he explain to you anything about the trumpet or was it just in general? No, just in general. I didn't know if he gave you any sort of lessons or?
No, I sure wish I could have picked up some of the things he knew. Uh huh.
I wonder if he knew much about chords or if it was all by ear or what?

Well, for what he was playing, he must have known something somehow. Art White was strictly a gift to him because he, well the same with Punch. Punch Miller was a guy that amazed me with what he could do with those three vows. Because his vows were, was one of these real fast-fingering things and there was a lot of, a lot of feeling to it. Not just a lot of notes, there was a lot of feeling coming out of the horn. And here's some of these trumpet players make all of these notes, a thousand notes. And there's no feeling coming, no feeling attached to it. But these guys had a lot of feeling and it was, and the guy that I thought had a tremendous feeling in his horn was Hippolyte Charles. Really?
Have you ever heard of him? I know him, but I never heard of him play because he quit long before.
Oh, but he was a beautiful trumpet player.
I guess he quit about the time I was born, you know. Really?
I didn't even know Hippolyte was still living until the other day. Somebody said yes, he's still living. He's out in Parks, Louisiana.
That's his home?
Yes.

I have his address if you want me to get it. Okay. Sounds good. And his phone number. You may be passing right by that. Right. Anyway, would you call Hippolyte a jazz musician or strictly a reader or just one who had both?
I'd just call him a good musician. He had both of them. Yeah.
Because I always, I didn't know how much jazz he played. He said he never, he must have played some to hear him tell you.
He had to play some. Yeah.
Everybody talks about him very often. This tape is almost over and I'll phone up and get Hippolyte Charles' address right now. I know that sounds good. Because we'll be closing in a few minutes.
If I don't do it now, we'll be in the middle of another tape. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. We'll be closing in a few minutes. Yeah. And now we'll be in the middle of another day. Yeah.
Okay, this is Don Albert, Real 2, December the 30th, 1969, I believe it is. Okay, I wanted to ask you about the arrangers in your band a little bit. Now, who did most of the arrangers?

Well, when the band first left here, when I organized it here in New Orleans, there weren't any arrangers. We would take the stocks and we would rearrange the stocks to fit what we wanted, and how we wanted it. But we were concentrating on our original style of playing. And the first arranger that I had in the band was a fellow out of Little Rock, Arkansas. He is still living today. His name is Philander Tiller, an alto player. Now, Phil was a tremendous arranger. And he could write arrangements that he couldn't read himself. He'd have to study them until he could play them. And I had Arthur Durbany, Lurie Cottrell, Urban Hall, and Phil Tiller. And, of course, as the band grew and the personnel changed, other arrangers came in. Cottrell finally got into the groove of writing an arrangement here and there. And so did Herbert Hall. And then later on, as we grew in size, we had a great arranger in the person of Harold Holmes, who was a bass player. And he's now in Canada. He wrote some tremendous arrangements for the band. And then we had the piano player, Lloyd Glenn, came in later times after Al Freeman, who was the first piano player. And Lloyd wrote arrangements. And we had little Billy Douglas to come in, the trumpet player, one of the greatest trumpet players I've ever heard in my life. He did some tremendous arrangements.
Did you ever hear him talk about Cuba? Cuban Bennett?
No, Bennett Douglas was a strange fellow. He never talked about anything in common. I remember you asking me about that, but no, he never mentioned anyone.
That's funny, because Alvin told me that they must have sat next to each other in the section or something. Alan who? Alvin Alcorn.

Oh, well, he and Alvin were good friends, yes. Now, if he mentioned it, well, we called him, when you said Alvin, I never would have known him. We called him Mickey. I never would have known it, because I never asked Mickey what the conversations were about.
What about the band's own ideas when you got an arrangement? How much would you change them?

The only things that would change in the band would be a few bad notes in there and had to correct the notes, but as far as the style of playing the solos, the men used their own ideas on their solos, but the arrangements were all rehearsed together.
Like a stock you wouldn't put your own stuff in that thing?
Just rearrange it to the feelings of the band and the men that were going to play it.
Let me see what else he wrote me, because I'll check Laurie Wright's letter here. What happened to the men with Troy Floyd? I forgot.

Well, it's quite, most of those fellas have passed. Those that are not passed, they are real elderly people now, and I imagine, the last time I saw Benny Long was about three years ago, and Benny's been awful sick. He hadn't had one of his legs cut off. Willie Long is dead. Charlie Dixon is dead. Troy Floyd is dead. The first piano player was named Leroy Moore, and I'm sure that he's gone.
Alan Vann was with him, huh?

Well, I got Alan Vann the job with him after Leroy Moore quit. See, I had a broad amount of, well, I don't know how you put it. Troy had depended on me to do things for him, and I would seek the musician, so I told him about Alan Vann's playing, and Troy was always a fella that you had to prove to him, or he never showed that he never was too interested in what you were talking about. So I had Alan to come and rehearse with the band at 520 South Hagbury, and he took him into the band from there. But I don't remember exactly how long the band stayed, but I think he stayed all the time that I was in the band. I quit the band in 1929, in Fort Worth, Texas.
Well, somebody in that band I was going to ask you about. Well, you only had John Alfred, the drummer. Oh, the guitar player.

Oh, John Henry Braggs. He's still living. He's in San Antonio. He doesn't play anymore. Did he sing the blues ever? No. Just played the banjo. He played an old-style banjo, what they call the plectrum banjo, five strings. Mm-hmm. Good musician. His wife was a blues singer, Ed L. Braggs.
I believe he may have recorded some himself, you know, later on. Maybe. I'll have to look it up.
I don't believe so. I believe after Troy's band disbanded, he might have done something with his wife in Fort Worth.
Yeah. That's what I'm thinking. That was his home, Fort Worth. Mm-hmm. I thought maybe they cut some blues together or something. I don't have the book with me. I don't believe it.
Yeah, they might have. I won't say he didn't.
Let's see if there's anything else we didn't go over. What kind of parts did Nick Turner play? Henry Turner, what was his name?
Nick, Nick played the tuba and doubled on the valve trombone in the brass section.
Mm-hmm. Did he play string bass at all?
No string bass. Just the valve trombone and the sousaphone.
And, uh, can you hear him on the recordings at all or no?
You, you can, you faintly can hear him on the recordings, very faintly.
Was he playing tuba or valve trombone?
No, he was playing tuba. Jimmy Johnson was playing string bass.

I've listened to him awful hard and I've never even noticed. Well, I can't. No, you can't hardly hear him. Well, Nick was a real soft man. Mm-hmm. I see. Must have been one of the first bands, one of the first, to use two basses, I guess.

First band, they used three basses. You had three basses? Two string basses and Nick on the tuba. Who were the string basses? Uh, old man, uh, Jimmy Johnson. Uh-huh. Uh, Harold Holmes. And Nick Turner. Where? First band to use the word swing.
You're talking about America's Greatest Swing Band. America's Greatest Swing Band. Well, how would those billings read? What would it say then?
Don Albert and his music. America's Greatest Swing Band.
And, of course, earlier you had another name.
Well, the first name was Don Albert and his Ten Pals.
Mm-hmm. And then his Ten Pals.
It grew into Don Albert and his Ten Pals, all 14 of them, which is a controversial name.
Mm-hmm. I guess that would attract people's attention and everything. That's right. Well, how often did you rehearse with that band?

Every time we could get a chance. You know, being a traveling band on the road and you stay up all night, you have to pick the times. And the times you were playing, maybe you had a couple of dates or you had a couple of days lay off. Well, I would call it a rehearsal and we'd rehearse that way. Or, if the guy, someone had heard an arrangement or a song they wanted to put an arrangement on, he would write it at intervals. And he'd let me know when it was ready. And, of course, I had Frank Jackie and Albert Martin and Cottrell in charge of most of the business. In fact, Cottrell was my business manager all the way through. And we would get together and see what we would call arrangements at a feasible place.
Mm-hmm. What would be a business manager, then?
Take care of little incidental and demand, such as bookkeeping, paying off the musicians, calling the rehearsals, and various things like that. And I would have time on the job, intermissions.
But would you cut out and go ahead and find a book?

Sometimes, sometimes I had to leave and go two or three weeks in front of the band to get bookings. Because my band should have been the number one band in the nation. I got tied up with the band Booker, Al Travis. God bless him wherever he is. And, when he got to New York, I was listening in the office and the guy told him, I said, Well, I understand that you have the greatest band to come out to South Alley, so I hope you stay straight. I never paid too much attention to it. I was too young a fella. And my whole ambition was to get to New York and get my band on the top. And I signed a contract with this fella. And he turned out to be one of the worst that I've ever known. I had to come back South and start all over again. And I would have to take the bookings in my hand and try to keep the bookings going and keep the band intact. Come back, be with the band another two, three, four weeks and leave again on another little tour to try to book some more dates.
Yeah, you mentioned that that had to do with the breaking up of the band.

Well, that happened in the later, later years. I broke up that one time right after Al Travis said to give us that bad booking. And I came back to New Orleans. I thought I wanted to quit. So, I'm being before you, I thought that some Negro agent came here and could make a tremendous, a lot of money for his boy. And I tried to explain what type of deal this was, but he went ahead and he let me have $4,000. And this proved to be a bad booker. I had to get rid of him, so I wanted to still keep the band after going through all of this with Furrier. To try to get it to pay off. And that's the reason why I stayed until 1940. Then in 1940, well, the musicians were getting so bad that they were quitting without notices. They were borrowing money, not paying back. And I just thought it was, it wasn't anything like my first band. When we had a bunch of gentlemen, we lived like brothers. And we did everything together. We shared money. We shared our sandwiches and our bread and everything together. And it was, it was always peace and honor. So I said, well, this isn't what I want. I just decided, well, I was going to quit. And that was in 1940. And Fats Martin picked up the remnants of my band and he just kept it at a level of five, six and seven pieces.
What about this Bernard Goldberg? Had you get in touch with him?

Well, Bernard Goldberg was an admirer of, he admired my playing and he thought that I would make a band leader. And he would come to Shadowland and he would ask me to organize a band. So I told him I wasn't ready. And when I came back here to New Orleans in, oh, it was 1929. But, Bernard came over and he said, why don't you get a band together? He says, I get you a real good job to start off with. I said, well, that sounds all right. He says, you need any money? He says, I'll give you a thousand dollars. So he gave me a thousand dollars. I got around here and got these guys together and they all decided it was a good deal. The first job was to stay for him in Dallas. And we all had brand new uniforms. Goldberg bought all of that. And I wish it would have been possible that I could have stayed with him because I believe if Goldberg had stayed with us, it would have been feasible for him and profitable for all of us. Because right behind him, we got another one named, oh, he's here in this town, Rabinowitz. He's mind the tire business, the men's wear tire. You might have met old Benowitz. He has a place right up there on where old Rampo Street used to come in. I don't know.
He sells tires.
Well, if you don't know him, so much the better.
So you try a lot of different bookers and you book the band yourself on judging from what you stand. That's right.
Well, you see, when the bookers would do bad and get rid of the bookers, then I had to go ahead and book them all.
And it's, it's, you already had that name, Don Albert. They were calling you Don before you organized your band?

Yes, and that's how I acquired the name. And as I told you before, I, of course, my wife disagrees with me. She seemed to think that the Dominic would have been as good or better name. But I thought by having a shorter name that it would be better just to say Don Albert. Which to some people are confusing. A lot of people don't know that Don Albert is Don Albert Dominic. See, they come to San Antonio looking for Albert Dominic in the form book and actually it's Don Albert. So they don't, they're confused.
Yeah, you wrote me that the guys in Troy Floyd's band called you Don.
I called me Don and Jim. Jim. I don't know whether Jim, I never will understand how Jim, Big Jim.
You know, I forget who it was. I think it's maybe Texas Tommy I came across recordings by. And it seemed to be members of the Troy Floyd band and it had a mandolin in there. I wrote you about that.
Yeah, that was made the day we made those records. And I know this to be a fact that, was it a tremendous mandolin solo or just mandolin chords?
It seemed to me it was very good, but I wouldn't swear to him.

Well, Caffrey Dallas, boy, was one of the greatest I ever heard. And he used to play up here with Manuel in the band at the old roof corner. With Manuel Borreiro. Right. And he left here and he went to Dallas. He sent him to Dallas and of course he sent for his brother later on Percy. Percy and I were good friends, but so was Caffrey and I. Caffrey was a genius. He was just like John Moreira. I don't know if you ever heard of John Moreira. Sure. John Moreira to me was the greatest banjo player I've ever heard in my life. And why? There's not so much said about John Moreira. I shall never know. Because he was a genius and so was Caffrey Darren's boy, either the mandolin or the guitar or the banjo.

So it may well have been him on that date. Yeah, I'm sure it does. I'm almost positive. You don't remember him being in the studio or anything? Yes, I do. You remember him being there? Yes, I do. Oh, well that's great. I'm glad to know.
Caffrey's been dead for years. His wife is still living in Dallas.
Yeah, well he had a sort of a bad life on the end.

He turned bad. He was a little fella. You know they say little people. Don't arouse them because they're bad. They feel as though you're taking advantage of their size. Well Caffrey got into the underworld business in Dallas by just about the time that I brought my little band there. And he was giving up his plane. Well he made lots of money in the type of business he was in. But by the same token, he ran into a lot of trouble. And he used his gun freely. That's how he died. Some fella shot him in the back.
No. No. Uh, let me see now. I wanted to ask you about that 1776.

Yeah. They didn't call me 1776. It was the box that I had, the little flip top box for my little cornet. And he's always a fella always wondered whatever happened to him. He was learning the clarinet about the same time as I was learning the trumpet. I mean the cornet. His name was Elliot Taylor. Uh huh. And I think he's the one that gave him that name.
Well he continued on. I know he played the name of him.
I know he did but I have never heard of him in the last 30, 40 years.
Wow. So many people moved away. That's right. And he was one that moved. Did you ever hear Kid Ory when you were a kid?
No, I can't ever recall what he and Ory played outside of his records. In fact, I didn't know Ory personally.
What about Duke Ellington? You know him personally?

Well sure. Duke and I are great friends. How'd that happen? Well, through Bonnie. Through Bonnie Biggore, my cousin. When they booked the tour in Texas, I wired Bonnie that I was there and I wanted them to be my guests at my house. So I met them in Austin, Texas, which is 75 miles from San Antonio and then I brought them into San Antonio. By the same token, cab the same way. In those days they had what they called the circuit where they played all of these theater dates. That's most of the dates that Ellington and Cab were playing. And then Touloui came to San Antonio if I remember when. Well, it was 1928, 27, 28. And I was responsible for these bookers getting them down there.
When did they have that flood there?
Recently?
No, in the 20s. Wasn't that a big flood? No. Not that I remember.
Yeah, it might have been before you got there. Might have been before, but there was a bad flood here a few years ago in the 50s. It almost washed my nightclub away.
But what about those band leaders when they came then, the musicians? Did they have trouble finding a place to stay? Well, sure they did.

They wouldn't let them go. Well, it was the same way, let me put it this way. The history of the Negro band, such as mine, on the road, is so tragic that sometimes you hate to even recall those days. Because you want to try to forget the things that were done to you. And you would come to town, the first place you would have to look for is the railroad track. Because you knew on the other side of the railroad track is where Negroes lived. And you would be welcomed into their homes over there. But the life of a Negro musician in the era that we came up was so, so bad that sometimes you hate to recall the things that were done to you. For instance, in Thomasville, Georgia, they wanted to lynch the whole band, my band. And Duke Ellington and Cab and Jimmie Lunsford and Andy Craig and all of us were together. You can imagine the hardships that we encountered. And sometimes to have enough to eat, me being as light as I am, I would go into the places and buy the sandwiches and bring them out so they could eat in the bus. Or maybe sometime it would have to send, I would go in the grocery store and buy a couple of loaves of bread and some lunch meats or something like that. That was our dinner, breakfast and supper. Which like I say to me, the memories to discuss this is so nauseating. And to me it touches me because I look back at those things and see how they have treated my people and me. I don't like to discuss it too much.
Well, I don't want to pressure you about that business in Thomasville or anything. We can talk about something else if you want to. Well, that's left to you.
I mean, I... If you want to.
I'd like to ask. Sure. I told you so. You know, you're one of the people that will be honest about things. Right, right, right. A lot of people won't.

Well, for instance, we thought that when we crossed the Mason and Dixon line, we always thought, well, hell, man, this is heaven. You know, we're going into this place here. We found more discrimination on the other side of the Mason and Dixon line than we found down here. Down here you knew where they say your place is. So that's the place that you seek to find. But up there you thought, well, everything was all right. And you find you get up there, you see a different picture altogether. And my band was one of the first Negro bands to play in some areas where they didn't want Negro bands to play due to the fact they thought that I was a white band leader. And we got in that way, but after we got to town and it was booked and all, we played the dances. So you? So I think that I set a precedent for the Negro bands that are coming up today. Well, we went to a place in Glens Falls, not in Glens Falls, New York, Sioux City Highway, in Pierre, North Dakota. And I went up to get some rooms. And when I got up to Adelaide, she said she had 10 rooms. I said, fine, got the price and all. I said, well, I'll go and get my musicians and bring them up. And we're going up the steps, another lady stopped me and she said, where are you going? I said, we're going to our room. She says, we don't have any rooms here. I said, sure you do. I just talked to the lady and she says, yeah, 10. I said, well, those rooms were rented just before you came up here.
What about Thomasville? Do you mind talking about that?

No, no. The reason for that is I had Tom Johnson in the band from here. I just hired Tom and I had a boy named Buddy Collins, who was a singer. And he started a fight in the auditorium that night of free-for-all. And I was on the front door with the principal of the school, taking care of the business and the money. They hurdled a whole band off in a paddy wagon, two girls I had that were dancers, the James sisters. Put them all in there. Of course, a few of the fellas got away. Mickey and I think it was Kato and bass player, a couple of others. Tom Johnson was playing trumpet. Brought us all to jail, locked us up in the jail. Called me all kind of nigger, smart nigger from New York. Took all the money. And when I asked him about going to court, he said, well, I'm setting this fine where the judge is going to set it. He says, the only thing you can do is this. There's an interest in the outlet to this town. I want you to use both of them. So, the other guys were missing. I told them I would go with them and help them find them. He told them I was too damn smart. And he told the fellas I was too small and nigger to be in front of them. In front of the band. And another policeman would come up there and snap the six-hute in my face six times. So, you can imagine 19 people in a small room, say 12 maybe. About 12 was as big as it was. But there's always one good fella in the world. You can't classify all white people in the same category. By the same token, you can't classify all Negroes as bad. We stopped at a service station. We were going to Macon, Georgia. And I asked the guy about getting some gas. I said, I need at least 150 gallons of gas. I'm going to Macon, Georgia. I don't have any money. Will you trust me until I get to Macon? He said, yes, I will. He said, you fellas was in trouble last night. I said, yes. And I also need five gallons of oil because the old busboy was a lot of oil. Well, the guy was real nice. He filled up both of the tanks and gave me five gallons of oil. When I got to Macon, Georgia, I widened back his money.
The demand wasn't involved in the fight or anything?

No. Well, in a way they were. There was a fella that jumped up on a stand and he wanted to do something to Tom Johnson. And Tom Johnson folded his sack stand and he hit this fella in the head. But I think all this was put up by the police to do this. And even they told the principal of the school that he came to my defense. He said, well, this man wasn't even around. So they said, you mean to tell me that you're a nigga here that lives in Thomasville, Jordan. You're going to take up for these niggas that come from out of town. I said, well, we'll get you fired in the morning. So the poor fella had to back off. There was nothing he could do. He was the principal of the school. And they took every dime I had. And they even make the girls, I'd give them the girls some money to put up in there. Apparently he used to hide it. They had them take it out and give it all to them.
What about Dominic? We got a couple of minutes. You say you're some Ken to him?

I talked to one of my cousins yesterday. She's an old woman and way up in the 80s, close to 90. Her name is Lucia Goyns, G-O-I-N-S. And she was a Tomatis. And her mother was my grandfather's sister. My grandfather didn't have any brothers. He came from the Dominican Republic as far as we can be told by these older people that live in the country. And so very few of them that live in the actual history. And he had a sister but no other brothers. And his daddy was the Dominic U, the captain of the fleet that Gene Lafitte was at the head of. And his tombstone is in the second graveyard, if I can remember well, in the center aisle. St. Louis is number two. And he's number one right up here on Claymore Street. And it's in the second door. And you have one, two, three. And it's in that middle aisle and it says Dominic U and it has the symbol of a mason. And I don't know why it is, but people never did like to discuss too much of a shady character, which they would consider a pirate a shady character. And I've always, often asked Zad Piran, who has the history of my family and my family tree. And she has a broad, broad memory, a great memory I'll say. And she didn't know too much about my grandfather. But this, Miss Lucia Goenz, is a sister to my grand, is a daughter of my grandfather's sister. And I intended to go back and talk to her, but my time is so short, Dick, when I come here, that I can't do the things that I would like to do. I was thinking that someday, maybe if I could sell my place of business in San Antonio, that I would come back here where I could spend a lot of time and research and do the things like that to actually get the things that I would like to know about the family tree.

You know, I've never understood, it brings me back to New Orleans, why somebody can be world famous and not make it in New Orleans, you know, musicians. It seems like they turn their back on me, this is off the subject.

Yeah, I never have been able to understand that myself. However, let me say this, that I have met up with a lot of great response when I had my band, when I came back to New Orleans, even though I was considered a Texas boy, by Texans and other people, but whenever I played here, the Santa Cendez was one of the places that I would just put thousands of people in. And also the old Tick Tock and the Pelican, we played those places by the time we tuned our horns up the line, was two blocks around to hit a Don Albert band.
Well, I'm not talking about the people, I just, it's funny, the attitude of night club owners and all that, I suspect, you know, that it's the same old race practice, it had something to do with it.

Well, in the past, it was so predominant here that a lot of times I dreaded coming back here. But now the trend is just a little bit different. But Dick, let me say this, that you're going to find this sort of people any way you go. When you're a Negro, you're just a Negro today. And times are not too much better, because I seem to want to be on the militant side, I have to be. I fought this thing and I fought prejudices in San Antonio, and I have letters from the governors, from the president, everyone else trying to get things for the Negroes settled right. But it's just a hatred, and I don't know what it is, within people that they just haven't been able to get rid of it. And until, until the day comes, when these things can be gotten out of a man's system, you're not going to have peace and harmony, nothing. It is known in the music, you find, of course it's predominant with you in the music because you follow this. But you can get in civil service such as I am and you'll find the same things that exist there.
It seems to me it's better in music than a lot of them. Yeah. A whole lot of people have been fighting racial prejudice for years, through music.
That's right, through music and sports. It's been the greatest medium.
Well, we only have a few seconds left, so I wanted to thank you again for everything, and I'm glad we got this done. I hope we can do a good article.

Well, I hope so, and I most certainly want you to read this article, or I'm going to give it to you. Now, Mario Maverick is an attorney, and he is a civil rights, he's a white attorney, but he is a civil rights advocate. And he has fought this thing down the line. That's the reason why you notice that the article will be pointing to why San Antonio doesn't recognize Don Albert any more than they do. You'll notice that it's not a direct accusation, but it's in there. Mm-hmm.

segments.title: Opening: name, date and location of interview
segments.summary: Albert gives his stage and full name, Don Albert Dominique, and the date, 30 December 1969, at the interviewer's apartment.

segments.title: First hearing Louis Armstrong in New Orleans parades
segments.summary: As a child Albert listened to parading boys' bands; he met Armstrong only later, after he had his own band, and they became close friends.

segments.title: Wabash Blues and the Troy Floyd recordings
segments.summary: Albert doubts Troy made Wabash Blues but has a copy and thinks he and Charlie Dixon played on it; the recordings took three or four days.

segments.title: Joining Troy Floyd's band in Texas at 17
segments.summary: Albert traces Floyd's band back to Alphonso Trent, tells how he left his three-piece band, and was hired on the spot without audition by Floyd.

segments.title: Head arrangements, stock arrangements and who read in Floyd's band
segments.summary: The band used many head arrangements and stocks; only a few could read, and Albert transposed parts from violin, clarinet or piano.

segments.title: Albert's musical family and Uncle Natty Dominique
segments.summary: Albert studied music and comes from a musical family; he talks about visiting his uncle Natty Dominique in Chicago.

segments.title: Changing stock arrangements and Charlie Dixon
segments.summary: Stocks were altered only in introductions and choruses; Albert recalls Charlie Dixon's death and his fatherly role in the band.

segments.title: Band personnel: Willie Long, Scott Bagby and turnover
segments.summary: Dixon's main instrument was tuba; Scott Bagby played piano by ear; Floyd's band had little turnover while Albert was there.

segments.title: Scott Bagby's nickname Funny
segments.summary: Bagby was nicknamed Funny because he was comical; the young musicians teased him and he blew his stack.

segments.title: Meeting Herschel Evans and teaching him to read
segments.summary: Albert met Evans in New Orleans, found him with a circus in Wichita Falls, put him in Floyd's band and taught him to read.

segments.title: Battles of bands and meeting Walter Page's Blue Devils
segments.summary: Battles of bands were a gate attraction; Albert recalls one with George E. Lee and meeting Page, Lips Page and Basie in Dallas.

segments.title: Floyd's gold orchestra, C.G. Conn horn and Floyd as leader
segments.summary: Floyd's orchestra had gold instruments; Albert was given a trumpet and rehearsals were frequent; Floyd had faults but was a nice man.

segments.chapter: Southwestern bands and New Orleans youth
segments.title: No brass bands outside New Orleans
segments.summary: Albert never heard a brass band outside New Orleans until Columbia, South Carolina, behind Daddy Grace.

segments.chapter: Southwestern bands and New Orleans youth
segments.title: Southwestern bands: Trent, Lazy Daddy and the Royal Garden Band
segments.summary: Troy and Trent were the main big bands; Edgar Perry led the little-remembered Royal Garden Band.

segments.chapter: Southwestern bands and New Orleans youth
segments.title: Troy Floyd's theme and showmanship
segments.summary: Floyd's theme was sung and spoken like Ted Lewis; he was more of a gimmick man but could get jobs.

segments.chapter: Southwestern bands and New Orleans youth
segments.title: George Moret, rough New Orleans trumpeter
segments.summary: Moret lived near Albert's family, read music and played loud and rough; Albert went on jobs with him at ten or twelve.

segments.chapter: Southwestern bands and New Orleans youth
segments.title: Playing professional jobs as a boy, lake boats and the nine o'clock whistle
segments.summary: His parents let him play jobs at about fourteen, and boat trips across the lake; his father blew a whistle to call him home.

segments.chapter: Southwestern bands and New Orleans youth
segments.title: Visiting Buddy in Covington and trumpet feeling
segments.summary: Albert visited Buddy in his shack in Covington to talk music; he admires the feeling of players like Punch Miller.

segments.chapter: Southwestern bands and New Orleans youth
segments.title: Hippolyte Charles and the end of tape one
segments.summary: Albert praises Hippolyte Charles' feeling, learns he lives in Parks, Louisiana, and the tape runs out.

segments.title: Arrangers in Albert's band
segments.summary: Albert lists arrangers Philander Tiller, Cottrell, Harold Holmes, Lloyd Glenn and Billy Douglas; stocks were rearranged but solos were free.

segments.title: What became of Floyd's musicians; Leroy Moore, Alan Vann, John Henry Braggs
segments.summary: Most of Floyd's men have died; Albert got Alan Vann the piano job, quit in 1929, and recalls banjoist John Henry Braggs.

segments.title: Basses in Albert's band: Nick Turner, Jimmy Johnson, Harold Holmes
segments.summary: Turner played tuba and valve trombone; the band used three basses.

segments.title: Band billing names and rehearsing on the road
segments.summary: From Don Albert and his Ten Pals to America's Greatest Swing Band; rehearsals were fitted into layoffs.

segments.title: Business manager, bad bookers and breaking up in 1940
segments.summary: Cottrell was business manager; a bad booker, Al Travis, wrecked plans, and Albert disbanded in 1940.

segments.title: Bernard Goldberg financing the first band
segments.summary: Goldberg gave $1,000 and uniforms to start the band in 1929; later bookers failed and Albert booked himself.

segments.title: How he got the name Don Albert, and Big Jim
segments.summary: Albert chose the shorter name Don Albert; Floyd's men called him Don and Big Jim.

segments.title: Mandolinist Caffrey Darensbourg and the Troy Floyd date
segments.summary: The mandolin on the record was likely Caffrey, a genius, like banjoist John Marrero; Caffrey later turned to the underworld and was shot.

segments.title: The 1776 nickname and Kid Ory
segments.summary: The nickname came from his cornet box via Elliot Taylor; Albert never knew Kid Ory personally.

segments.title: Bringing Ellington and Cab Calloway to San Antonio
segments.summary: Through cousin Barney Bigard, Albert hosted Ellington and Cab in San Antonio and helped book them.

segments.title: Hardships of Black bands on the road
segments.summary: Black bands sought homes by the railroad tracks; Albert bought food, and found northern discrimination and hotel refusals.

segments.title: Jailed in Thomasville, Georgia
segments.summary: A fight at a dance led to the band's arrest, extorted fines and threats; a station owner trusted him for gas to Macon.

segments.title: Dominique family history
segments.summary: Albert recounts his grandfather's Dominican origins and a pirate ancestor connected to Lafitte, and the family tree.

segments.title: Reception in New Orleans, prejudice and music
segments.summary: Albert drew crowds in New Orleans clubs but recalls prejudice there and in San Antonio, and says music and sports have fought it.

segments.title: Closing thanks and San Antonio recognition
segments.summary: The interviewer thanks him; Albert mentions an article on San Antonio's lack of recognition and attorney Maury Maverick.
